summary: Gives guidance on when a Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) router should implement a restart mechanism and which approach suits which situation. It is an applicability statement, so it advises rather than defining new protocol machinery. It covers the restart issues also relevant to constraint-based LSP setup in RFC 3212.

plainLanguage.summary: When a worker takes a quick break, you want the factory line to keep moving. This note helps decide when network routers need a plan to keep traffic flowing while one restarts, and which plan fits best.

questions: when to use ldp graceful restart
how do routers recover from failure
subtitle: Guidance on when network routers need recovery plans for label distribution failures.

tldr.problem: When routers managing MPLS label distribution fail or restart, they lose track of which labels go to which paths, disrupting traffic. Recovery requires coordinating with neighboring routers to restore the correct state.
tldr.mechanism: Two approaches are available: Graceful Restart, where routers relearn what their neighbors know, and Fault Tolerance, where routers acknowledge each label change so they can quickly confirm what survived the failure.
tldr.outcome: Choosing the right approach depends on the scenario (a link failure versus a full restart), whether forwarding continues, and how quickly recovery must happen.

today: RFC 3612 is Informational and has not been obsoleted. It remains the reference for choosing between LDP restart mechanisms, though implementation choices are left to vendors and operators.

sections.title: The Challenge of Router Restarts
sections.content:
Multiprotocol Label Switching (MPLS) is a way to route data through networks using short labels instead of long IP addresses. A Label Distribution Protocol (LDP) router must remember which labels map to which data paths. When a router fails or restarts, it loses this memory, and its neighbors do not know whether it still has the forwarding state needed to keep traffic flowing.

The RFC addresses two kinds of problems: a temporary failure of the communication link between two neighboring routers (session failure), and a complete restart of one of the routers (node failure). In both cases, procedures are needed to prevent the loss of active traffic flows.
sections.plainLanguage: A router keeps a list of which short names (labels) go with which paths. When it crashes or restarts, it forgets the list. It needs a way to remember it or ask its neighbors what it lost.

sections.title: The Two Recovery Approaches
sections.content:
Two extension mechanisms have been proposed to help routers recover from failures. The first approach, Graceful Restart (RFC 3478), lets a restarting router relearn its state from its neighbors. The router tells its peers it is restarting and asks them to re-advertise the labels they previously sent.

The second approach, Fault Tolerance (RFC 3479), is more complex. Routers acknowledge each label message as it arrives and keep checkpoints of the current state. When a failure occurs, they know exactly which messages were confirmed before the break and can quickly restore only what survived.
sections.plainLanguage: Graceful Restart is like asking your coworkers to repeat the parts list. Fault Tolerance is like taking snapshots of the parts list every few minutes so you can restore from the latest snapshot.

sections.title: Session Failure versus Node Failure
sections.content:
Session Failure is when the communication link between two routers breaks, but both routers are still running. Both routers can hold onto their label state and simply need to reconnect and verify what survived. Both approaches (Graceful Restart and Fault Tolerance) work well here.

Node Failure is when one entire router restarts or crashes. That router loses everything unless it specifically saved state before the restart. Graceful Restart can still work because the restarting router relearns state from its neighbors. Fault Tolerance requires that the restarting router kept some checkpoint data; without it, it cannot help.

A Controlled Failure is when the operator knows a failure is coming (a planned maintenance or upgrade). In this case, Fault Tolerance allows time to checkpoint the state and quiesce the link before shutdown, making recovery faster.
sections.plainLanguage: If just the phone line breaks but both people are still there, either method works. If one person has a heart attack, Graceful Restart is better because the healthy person can remind the recovering person. Fault Tolerance works if the person had written everything down before fainting.

sections.title: When to Use Each Approach
sections.content:
The choice depends on several factors. If the network changes labels frequently (reacting to routing changes), Fault Tolerance with its acknowledgement system can preserve more state. If changes are rare and bursty, Graceful Restart's simpler resynchronization is often sufficient.

Graceful Restart has no impact on normal operations and is simpler to implement. Fault Tolerance requires acknowledging every label message, which adds overhead in very busy networks. Graceful Restart works even if only one side of the router pair implements it, making it better for mixing old and new routers. Fault Tolerance requires both sides to implement the extensions.

For controlled shutdowns (maintenance), Fault Tolerance is faster because checkpointing and quiescing can complete all state transfer before the shutdown. For unplanned failures, both approaches take roughly the same recovery time but require different preparation.
sections.plainLanguage: Pick Graceful Restart if the network is simple and compatible with older equipment. Pick Fault Tolerance if you need speed and can plan shutdowns, or if labels change all the time.

sections.title: Where These Techniques Stand
sections.content:
RFC 3612 is an applicability statement, not a protocol definition. It advises when and where the restart mechanisms defined in RFC 3478 and RFC 3479 are suitable. Both RFCs have been standardized. Graceful Restart (RFC 3478) is favored in networks that mix equipment from different vendors, while Fault Tolerance (RFC 3479) is deployed where recovery speed and traffic preservation are critical.

The choice also applies to Constraint-based LSP Setup (CR-LDP, defined in RFC 3212), which has different label distribution modes and its own restart needs.
sections.plainLanguage: This is a guide, not a rule. Both methods work. Network operators use this RFC to pick the best one for their situation.
